lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: Well, Alexander, you can hardly deny that you're my son now. If you were Ammon's, you wouldn't be dead.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I never doubted it myself, Father. I knew I was the son of Philip, son of Amyntas. I just accepted the oracle because I thought it would be useful for the campaign.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: What? You thought it was useful to let a bunch of prophets make a fool out of you?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: Not that. But it terrified the barbarians. None of them would stand and fight because they thought they were up against a god. It made them much easier to beat.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: Beat? What men worth fighting did you ever beat? You were constantly up against cowards hiding behind little bows, tiny target-shields, and wicker bucklers! Defeating Greeks—now that was work. Subduing Boeotians, Phocians, Athenians; routing the Arcadian heavy infantry, the Thessalian cavalry, the javelin-throwers of Elis, or the Mantinean peltasts; handling Thracians, Illyrians, Paeonians—those are real achievements. But Medes, Persians, Chaldeans? Soft men dripping in gold? Don't you know that the Ten Thousand under Clearchus marched right in and beat them long before you did? The Persians didn't even wait for hand-to-hand combat. They ran before they were in bowshot!

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: But what about the Scythians, Father? And the Indian elephants? That was no trivial feat. And I beat them without dividing them against each other, or buying my victories with treason. I never broke an oath, or lied about a promise, or played false just to win. As for the Greeks, I took some over without shedding a drop of blood—and you've probably heard how I dealt with the Thebans.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: Oh, I know all about it. Cleitus told me. You know, the man you ran through with a spear in the middle of dinner because he dared to say my achievements were better than yours. [pause] And you threw off the Macedonian cloak and put on Persian robes, so they tell me. You wore the upright tiara, and expected Macedonians—free men!—to prostrate themselves before you. The most ridiculous thing of all was aping the manners of the very people you'd defeated. I won't even mention the rest of it: locking educated men in cages with lions, those marriages of yours, your extravagant devotion to Hephaestion. I only approved of one thing I heard: that you kept your hands off Darius's beautiful wife, and took proper care of his mother and daughters. That, at least, was the conduct of a king.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: But don't you praise my willingness to take risks, Father? Being the first one over the wall at the city of the Oxydracae, and taking all those wounds?

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: No, Alexander, I do not. Not because I don't think it's a fine thing for a king to take a wound now and then, and to lead his army from the front. But because, in your case, it was utterly counterproductive! You were pretending to be a god. Taking a wound, being carried off the battlefield on a litter, bleeding, groaning in pain... it was a joke to anyone watching! It exposed Ammon as a fraud, his oracle as a fake, and your prophets as flatterers. Who wouldn't laugh, seeing the son of Zeus fainting and begging the doctors for help? Even now that you're dead, don't you think there are plenty of people mocking your whole charade, looking at the corpse of a god laid out flat, rotting and swelling up just like any other body? And besides, Alexander, this "useful trick" of yours—the shortcut to victory—it robbed your actual achievements of their glory. When people think a god is doing the conquering, human accomplishment looks cheap.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: That's not what people think of me! They rank me right alongside Heracles and Dionysus. In fact, I was the only one who captured the Rock of Aornus—neither of them could do it!

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: [sighs] You see? You're still talking like the son of Ammon. Comparing yourself to Heracles and Dionysus! Have you no shame, Alexander? Will you never unlearn this vanity, know yourself, and realize that you're dead?
